fetched_contents.text: China in Greece: The Story of Piraeus and Beyond – chinaobservers This article is based on the final thesis of the General Diplomatic Training Program at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Czech Republic, titled “From Belgrade to Piraeus: China’s Strategy in Southeast Europe.” Over the past two decades, China has evolved from a regional powerhouse into a global actor. Europe – and Southeast Europe in particular – has become a key arena for Beijing’s ambitions. The region serves not only as a commercial gateway to the European Union but also as a stage where Chinese investments, political engagement, and public diplomacy converge. Among the countries of Southeast Europe, Greece stands out. Its strategic location, EU membership, and financial vulnerability during the debt crisis made it a testing ground for Beijing’s long-term strategy. This article examines China-Greece relations, focusing on the Port of Piraeus – the flagship project of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in Europe – and offers a brief comparison with Serbia to highlight the contrasting nature of Chinese investments and the differing public perceptions they generate. China-Greece Relations: An Overview China and Greece formalized a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2006, laying the groundwork for intensified cooperation in trade, infrastructure, and maritime transport. Symbolism has also played a role: both sides frequently invoke their “ancient civilizations” as a cultural bridge. Yet the primary driver has been economic necessity. The relationship remained strong in 2024, with bilateral trade reaching roughly €12.6 billion, and Greece continuing to present China as a reliable partner – not only in infrastructure but also in emerging areas such as green technology and the digital economy. For Beijing, Greece provided an entry point into the European market. For Athens, Chinese investment during the austerity years provided a much-needed economic lifeline. Over the past 15 years, Chinese companies have invested more than €10 billion, primarily in shipping, energy, telecommunications, and real estate. Beijing has also supported Greek shipowners, who transport a significant share of Chinese exports, while thousands of Chinese citizens have entered Greece through the Golden Visa program. Politically, Greece’s approach has fluctuated. During the crisis years, Chinese investments were warmly received. Under Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras, Athens even blocked an EU statement critical of Beijing at the UN in 2017. Later governments adjusted course: Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis strengthened ties with the EU and the United States, restricted Huawei’s role in the 5G rollout, and adopted a more cautious stance. Nonetheless, Greece continues to present itself as a bridge between East and West – open to Chinese investment, but within European strategic boundaries. Public opinion reflects this ambivalence. According to 2024 Pew Research data, nearly half of Greeks view China positively, while a similar share remains skeptical. Trust in President Xi Jinping is low, and concerns persist about overreliance on Chinese capital. Unlike in Serbia, the Greek government does not heavily politicize Chinese projects, leaving public attitudes more divided. Piraeus: China’s Flagship in Europe The Port of Piraeus epitomizes both the opportunities and limits of Chinese investment in the EU. In 2008, China’s state-owned shipping giant COSCO secured a concession to operate two of the port’s three terminals. In 2016, it acquired a majority stake in the Piraeus Port Authority for €1.5 billion, pledging a further €550 million in investments to modernize the port and transform it into a logistics hub for Europe. The results are significant: Piraeus has become one of the busiest ports in the Mediterranean and a critical hub for Chinese goods entering Europe. Employment has increased, container throughput has multiplied, and Athens has gained international visibility as a maritime hub. Chinese shipping and Greek shipowners remain closely intertwined, reinforcing the economic partnership. However, the project also reveals constraints and controversies. Expansion into adjacent sectors, such as rail transport, has stalled due to EU competition rules. COSCO has faced opposition from local unions and residents concerned about labor rights, environmental damage, and limited local economic spillover. Critics argue that while the port thrives as a transit point, Greece has not fully captured added value from logistics and processing activities. Piraeus thus stands as both a success story and a cautionary tale – evidence that Chinese firms can modernize strategic infrastructure, but also a reminder that EU regulations and local resistance can curb Beijing’s ambitions. fetched_contents.text: Piraeus Port rises on back of stronger ties Since China COSCO Shipping Corp officially took over its operations a decade ago, Piraeus Port in Greece has transformed from an aging facility into a highly coordinated global hub, achieving remarkable growth in capacity, revenue and technological advancement. In 2016, the annual container throughput of the port was approximately 680,000 TEUs (twenty-foot equivalent units), ranking 93rd globally with outdated facilities and limited capacity. Today, it has become one of the busiest ports in the Mediterranean, with annual throughput exceeding 5.6 million TEUs, ranking as high as 25th globally. Over the past decade, the transformation of the port's "hard power" has been the most intuitive. Terminals have been continuously extended, deep-water channels dredged, automated equipment gradually put into use, and bridge cranes and yard systems constantly upgraded. The once scattered and inefficient operational scenes have gradually transformed into a highly coordinated modern operating system. Piraeus Port has now become the fourth-largest container port, the second-largest cruise homeport, and the largest ferry port in Europe, as well as an important roll-on/roll-off automobile hub and ship repair center in the Eastern Mediterranean. "These 10 years mark the decade in which the port of Piraeus moved from a corner of the Mediterranean to a global hub," said Han Chao, chairman of the port operator Piraeus Port Authority SA. In recent years, the port's revenue and profit have continued to grow, reversing a long-term trend of losses. COSCO Shipping has invested over 10 billion yuan ($1.47 billion) locally, creating thousands of direct jobs and generating tens of thousands of indirect employment opportunities. "It has changed not only the port itself, but also the relationship between the city and its people," said Yannis Moralis, mayor of Piraeus. According to the recently released financial report of Piraeus Port Authority, the company's total revenue in 2025 reached approximately 251 million euros ($295.5 million), a year-on-year increase of 8.6 percent; operating profit stood at 132 million euros, up 2.2 percent year-on-year. Savvas Sanozidis, secretary of the board of directors of Piraeus Port Authority, said the transmission and integration of COSCO Shipping's corporate values have effectively strengthened supervision over management, promoting transparency, prudence and a high sense of responsibility in all aspects of work, providing a strong guarantee for the company's long-term sustainable development. Stefanos Gkikas, deputy minister of maritime affairs and insular policy of Greece, stated that the fruitful cooperation between COSCO Shipping and Piraeus Port Authority over the past decade has significantly enhanced the port's competitiveness and further consolidated Greece's position in the international shipping sector. The development path of the port is also quietly transforming. Stepping into the office building of the container terminal, one can see large screens displaying vessel dynamics, operational progress, and equipment status in real time. According to Han, the port has built a digital monitoring platform covering the entire port area and introduced 5G and artificial intelligence technologies, driving the production organization method to evolve from "manual planning" to "intelligent coordination". Looking ahead to the next decade, the development blueprint for Piraeus Port is clearly defined. "The future port will be smarter and greener," Han added. According to Han, the construction of the COSCO Shipping Piraeus Port park project was officially launched in April. fetched_contents.text: Chinese Investment in the Port of Piraeus Introduction Chinese investment in European strategic infrastructure has become a point of contention, particularly when the pursuit of economic benefits intersects with questions of strategic autonomy and foreign political influence. The Port of Piraeus in Greece has become a prominent example in this debate. Since the entry of the state-owned China Ocean Shipping Company (COSCO), the port has been integrated into China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). During a 2019 visit, Xi Jinping referred to Piraeus as the 'head of the dragon' of the BRI, signalling its perceived strategic importance within China’s European connectivity strategy. These developments have not gone unnoticed, and in December 2025, the U.S. Ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, suggested that China could be encouraged to divest parts of its stake. The U.S. has pledged to invest in the port of Elefsina, a port approximately 20 kilometres northwest of Piraeus, which is widely interpreted as an effort to counterbalance Chinese influence in the region. This article examines the economic and political consequences of Chinese investment in the Piraeus Port Authority (PPA), focusing on the benefits, drawbacks, and broader strategic implications for Greece and the European Union. By situating developments at Piraeus alongside Europe’s policy responses, it shows how investments in critical infrastructure can generate local economic benefits while simultaneously giving rise to strategic and geopolitical risks in Europe’s relationship with China. The Port of Piraeus The Port of Piraeus had been a state-run enterprise until 1999, after which the PPA became a publicly traded company, with the state remaining the majority stakeholder. In an effort to increase competitiveness, the Greek government initiated further liberalisation of the port in 2006. Following a period of negotiation and competitive bidding, the Greek authorities concluded a concession agreement with COSCO in 2008. The agreement granted COSCO the right to operate Pier II and to build and operate a new Pier III, while Pier I remained under the control of the PPA. It involved a total investment of 4.3 billion EUR, with operations commencing in 2009. As ports play a central role in managing the inflow and outflow of traded goods, COSCO’s position at the Port of Piraeus must be understood within the broader context of EU–China trade relations. COSCO, a Chinese state-owned international shipping company, ranks as the world’s fourth-largest shipping firm. China is the EU’s largest trading partner overall, its leading source of imports, and its third largest export destination. In this context, COSCO’s presence at a major European port places it in a position to influence the organisation of inbound and outbound container traffic at Piraeus. The timing of the deal coincided closely with the onset of the Eurozone crisis and its aftermath. As Greece entered a period of severe financial distress, a Troika composed of the European Commission, the European Central Bank, and the International Monetary Fund pushed for market-driven privatisations as part of its crisis management strategy. This approach significantly constrained alternative financing options, creating a policy dilemma for Athens. Within this policy environment, Chinese actors increasingly emerged as buyers of strategically important national assets. Chinese planners capitalised on these circumstances by acquiring critical infrastructure such as ports, energy networks, and transport systems at favourable prices, later integrating them into the BRI’s broader connectivity framework. In the case of Piraeus, the port’s connection to the railway network in 2013 proved particularly significant, accelerating its transformation into a key transit hub and logistics centre for the expanding Asia–Europe trade. Under the conditions attached to the Troika’s bailout programmes, the Greek government was left with little choice but to pursue further privatisation of the port. When it launched an international tender to sell 67% of the PPA, COSCO was the only company to submit a bid. The company benefited from particularly favourable terms, as the original agreement was revised twice during the financial crisis to safeguard COSCO’s profitability. In 2016, it consequently won the tender and acquired an initial 51% stake in the PPA for 280.5 million EUR. Greece formally joined the BRI in 2018, after which COSCO finalised the acquisition of the remaining 16% stake for 88 million EUR in 2021, subject to further mandatory investment commitments. Although the Greek government retained a seat on the board of directors, COSCO thus became the majority shareholder of the PPA, moving beyond its previous role as a concession holder. Economic Effects for Greece and the Region Chinese investments have significantly transformed the Port of Piraeus. It moved from outside the top 15 European harbours in 2007 in terms of container traffic volume, measured in twenty-foot equivalent units, to fourth place by 2019. Over this period, volume increased by 271.4%, compared to 57.9% of the second largest grower, Valencia. Moreover, the materials used for the port’s expansion came largely from China, reducing the need for European states to allocate public resources to the project. The expansion also generated approximately 1,000 local jobs and relied extensively on cooperation with local managers and subcontractors, while management involved only a small number of Chinese executives. Following the Chinese investment and cooperation with local businesses, several reports have suggested that Chinese management of Piraeus has produced positive spillover effects for the Greek economy, including substantial tax revenues for both local and national authorities. No. 4 (GR) September 2024 The Port of Piraeus as a Model of Greek-Chinese Cooperation Ioannis E. Kotoulas Introduction China and Greece are two major maritime nations and historical sea-oriented civilizations that lay special emphasis on the maritime dimension of economic and technological ties. China is a global leader in shipbuilding, in import and export of goods and procuring for global supply chains. Greece, strategically located on the geographical junction of Europe, Asia, and Africa, is the world’s largest shipping country, with a rich tradition of maritime activities, an impressive feat in itself. Maritime cooperation between China and Greece is essential aspect of China-Greece excellent ties and future relations. The port of Piraeus in continental Greece is the most important Greek port and a gateway for China into the European markets. After the cooperation with Chinese conglomerate COSCO was established in the early 21st century, Piraeus has marked an impressive rise surpassing other European ports in traffic and rising from 17th busiest port in 2007 to 4th busiest port in Europe in 2023. The port of Piraeus has become the most important port in the Mediterranean Sea, a focal point in Eurasian economic networks and is poised to become a global-scale hub for economic flows. Piraeus, an ancient port as part of the Maritime Silk Road Piraeus is an iconic port in Greek history. In ancient times, it used to be the port of the city of Athens, itself located inland. The city nexus and the port were connected with a 15km-long wall built to enhance the autonomy of Athens against its then rival, Sparta. Back in ancient times, Greek historian Thucydides (5th c. BC) had written that Piraeus was the port where “from all the lands, everything enters’’. As we shall see in detail below, cooperation with China over the last 15 years has revived this ancient potential. In modern times, Piraeus gained in importance again, especially after Athens rose again as the new capital of the Modern Greek state since 1833. The general turmoil of the late 19th and early 20th century did not allow for the realization of the potential of the port. The Piraeus Port Authority was established as a state owned company in 1930, in an attempt to increase Greek orientation towards the Mediterranean. In the 1970s, the spatial development of the port’s terminals effectively altered the image and the dynamics of the ports. The Piraeus Container Terminal and the shipbuilding zone are located in Perama, the car terminal is located in Keratsini-Drapetsona and the passenger port is located in Piraeus proper. Greece is a sea-oriented country due to its geophysical formation, its geographical location, its expertise and its economic orientation. Greece features an extended coastline with many suitable ports. The Aegean Sea is the intermediate sea hub between the closed Black Sea, the Mediterranean Sea and the semi-closed Adriatic Sea. Greece with its unique and advantageous geographical position and geophysical formation is a focal part of the One Belt One Road (OBOR) project and especially of the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. The OBOR project has been a signature initiative of Chinese President Xi Jinping that aspires to unite the great economic space of Eurasia, bringing together over 63% of the world’s population and 30% of the total global output. This project is based on a series of land and maritime routes. The land routes are the Northern Route (China-Central Asia-Russia to Europe), the Middle Route with two variations (China-Central Asia-Caspian Sea-Caucasus-Black Sea-Europe and China-Central Asia-Caspian Sea-Persian Gulf and Mediterranean Sea) and the Southern Route (China to Southeast Asia, South Asia and Indian Ocean). The two main sea routes constitute the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. The first one leads from the Chinese coastal cities via South China Sea to Indian Ocean and up to Europe (this is the route to Piraeus) and the second one leads from China via South China Sea to the South Pacific. Fig. 1: The 21st Century Maritime Silk Road and Greece’s focal position The international economic system remains to a large degree sea-oriented and dependent on maritime economic flows. Maritime transports are 75% cheaper than land transports and usually not susceptible to geopolitical tension between states due to the international character of open seas. Still, over the last period, the importance of land routes is also increasing, especially in the context of Eurasian continental connectivity. In the context of the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road ports like Piraeus are focal economic hubs and logistics nodes in a global network of interconnected areas. The Greek port of Piraeus is a perfect example in this regard. The port of Piraeus is located strategically on the Suez Canal-Gibraltar shipping route; it offers access to the Black Sea and the Balkan hinterland as an entry point towards Central and Eastern Europe through the railway system. Greeks have been very dynamic in terms of the maritime industry even before modern Greece was founded in 1830 and remain even today. The numbers are impressive. Piraeus’s regional logistics role has changed from a relatively minor Mediterranean port into a major gateway for South and East European trade, a central node for Greece, the Balkans, and the eastern Mediterranean, and a more prominent transshipment hub. The evidence points to Piraeus as a gateway for Chinese-linked supply chains and for broader European trade flows, but it also shows that its transformation was shaped by Greece’s strategic location and the port’s improved connectivity.

First, Piraeus is now clearly a key gateway for South and East European trade. The source material says that Piraeus has moved from outside the top 15 European harbours in 2007 to fourth place by 2019 in container traffic volume, and that its transformation into a key transit hub was accelerated by its railway connection in 2013 [N5-F3]. It is also described as a focal point in Eurasian economic networks and as poised to become a global-scale hub for economic flows [N6-F4]. The port’s location on the Suez Canal-Gibraltar shipping route and its access to the Black Sea and the Balkan hinterland through the railway system further supports its role as a gateway for South and East Europe [N6-F4]. The evidence also states that Piraeus offers access to the Black Sea and the Balkan hinterland as an entry point towards Central and Eastern Europe through the railway system [N6-F4]. This makes it especially relevant for trade flowing into Central and Eastern Europe from Asia, the Middle East, and the Mediterranean.

Second, Piraeus connects Greece, the Balkans, and the eastern Mediterranean more effectively than before. The historical narrative emphasizes Greece’s strategic position on the geographical junction of Europe, Asia, and Africa and notes that Piraeus has become a focal point in Eurasian economic networks [N6-F4]. The same source also highlights that Piraeus is located strategically on the Suez Canal-Gibraltar shipping route and provides access to the Black Sea and the Balkan hinterland [N6-F4]. The European Guanxi source adds that the port’s connection to the railway network in 2013 proved particularly significant, accelerating its transformation into a key transit hub and logistics centre for the expanding Asia–Europe trade [N5-F3]. This infrastructure connection means Piraeus can serve not only Greece but also the Balkans and the eastern Mediterranean more directly, supporting trade that passes through Athens to the broader European hinterland.

Third, Piraeus supports several important trade corridors and routes. The evidence points to Piraeus as a gateway for Chinese goods into Europe and as a logistics hub for European trade [N6-F4]. It is also described as a Mediterranean shipping hub, a strategic entry point for trade routes, and a port that is resilient to disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict on global supply chains [N4-R4]. The port’s role as a gateway for Chinese-linked supply chains is explicit in the China-CEE Institute briefing, which says Piraeus is a gateway for China into the European markets and a focal point in Eurasian economic networks [N6-F4]. In addition, the port is positioned as a transshipment hub because it connects the Mediterranean with the Black Sea and the Balkans via rail, and because it is part of a broader network of interconnected areas [N6-F4]. The Piraeus Port Authority itself offers reliable and efficient logistics and combined transport solutions, including direct rail connections [N3-R2]. These features make it better suited to support trade corridors linking Asia, the Middle East, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, and Central/Eastern Europe.

Fourth, Piraeus has become a transshipment hub and regional logistics node. The direct evidence is strong on this point. The European Guanxi source says that COSCO’s position at Piraeus places it in a position to influence the organisation of inbound and outbound container traffic at the port [N5-F3]. It also states that the port moved from outside the top 15 European harbours in 2007 to fourth place by 2019, with volume increasing by 271.4% compared to 57.9% for the second-largest grower, Valencia [N5-F3]. The China-CEE Institute briefing similarly frames Piraeus as a focal economic hub and logistics node in a global network of interconnected areas [N6-F4]. The Piraeus Port Authority’s logistics offerings, including combined transport solutions and direct rail connections, further support its role as a regional logistics node [N3-R2]. Overall, Piraeus has evolved from a regional seaport into a transshipment and logistics hub that strengthens the flow of goods through the eastern Mediterranean and into Central and Eastern Europe [N3-R4].

In summary, Chinese investment did not merely add capacity; it helped Piraeus become a more integrated regional logistics node. The port’s expanded role is tied to Greece’s strategic geography, its improved railway and maritime connectivity, and the growing importance of Piraeus as a gateway for both Chinese-linked supply chains and broader European trade flows [N6-F4][N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that Piraeus is now better positioned to serve South and East Europe, the Balkans, and the eastern Mediterranean as a transshipment hub, not just as a traditional port of call [N3-R2][N4-R4].

Chinese investment has transformed Piraeus’s operational and infrastructure capacity in several ways: it funded major infrastructure projects, accelerated terminal modernization and expansion, improved handling capacity and terminal efficiency, and introduced digitization and management reforms. The evidence also suggests that there are mixed signals about workforce and operational efficiency gains, with clear improvements in throughput and coordination but some concerns about local economic spillover and dependency.

First, major infrastructure projects were funded or accelerated. The most direct evidence is that COSCO acquired a majority stake in the Piraeus Port Authority in 2016 for €1.5 billion and pledged further €550 million in investments [N1-F1]. The European Guanxi source states that the port moved from an aging facility into a highly coordinated global hub, with terminals extended, deep-water channels dredged, automated equipment gradually put into use, and bridge cranes and yard systems constantly upgraded [N2-F2]. It also notes that COSCO has invested over 10 billion yuan ($1.47 billion) locally and that the construction of the COSCO Shipping Piraeus Port park project officially began in April [N2-F2]. The Accountability Toolkit entry mentions the upgrading and expansion of Pier I of Piraeus Port, at the Ikonion Container Terminal in Attica region, to provide extra capacity [N2-R4]. Together, these sources indicate that Chinese investment accelerated major port upgrades, including new terminal construction, dredging, and the expansion of existing infrastructure.

Second, handling capacity and terminal efficiency improved substantially. Piraeus’s container throughput grew from around 680,000 TEUs in 2016 to over 5.6 million TEUs, with the port ranked as high as 25th globally [N2-F2]. The port became one of the busiest in the Mediterranean, the fourth-largest container port, the second-largest cruise homeport, and the largest ferry port in Europe [N2-F2]. The European Guanxi source attributes this growth to the port’s transformation into a highly coordinated modern operating system, with once scattered and inefficient operational scenes gradually becoming highly coordinated [N2-F2]. The same source also says that COSCO’s corporate values strengthened supervision over management, promoting transparency, prudence, and a high sense of responsibility [N2-F2]. These improvements suggest that Chinese investment helped Piraeus move from an inefficient terminal system to one with much higher handling capacity and more efficient operations.

Third, modernization and digitization have evolved over time. The evidence shows a clear trajectory from manual planning to intelligent coordination. The European Guanxi source states that the port built a digital monitoring platform covering the entire port area and introduced 5G and artificial intelligence technologies, driving production organization from manual planning to intelligent coordination [N2-F2]. It also notes that the port has a modern waterfront space for leisure, sports, and social activities, as part of the new park project [N2-R2]. This indicates that Piraeus has moved beyond traditional port modernization into digital and smart-port infrastructure, with real-time vessel and operational monitoring, 5G, and AI playing a role in operations [N2-F2]. The port’s digital transformation is part of its broader move toward a “smart green” model [N2-R3].

Fourth, the evidence for workforce and operational efficiency gains is mixed but generally positive. The European Guanxi source states that COSCO’s investment created thousands of direct jobs and generated tens of thousands of indirect employment opportunities [N2-F2]. It also reports that the port’s revenue and profit have continued to grow, reversing a long-term trend of losses [N2-F2]. However, the same source warns that the project reveals constraints and controversies, including opposition from local unions and residents concerned about labor rights, environmental damage, and limited local economic spillover [N1-F1]. The China-CEE Institute briefing similarly notes that Piraeus is now a gateway for China into the European markets and a focal point in Eurasian economic networks [N6-F4], while the European Guanxi source argues that Piraeus has become a success story but also a cautionary tale, showing that Chinese firms can modernize strategic infrastructure but that EU regulations and local resistance can curb Beijing’s ambitions [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence supports real operational and workforce gains, but it also suggests that efficiency gains were not uniformly distributed across the local economy or workforce.

Overall, Chinese investment transformed Piraeus’s infrastructure capacity through major port projects, expanded handling capacity, improved terminal efficiency, and digital modernization. The evidence is strongest on the scale of investment, throughput growth, and operational coordination, but it also cautions that some local concerns and regulatory constraints remain [N2-F2][N1-F1].

After Chinese investment, Piraeus has become strategically important as a regional logistics hub for Chinese-linked supply chains, while also affecting Greece’s strategic autonomy and EU connectivity. At the same time, the port remains subject to risks and dependencies, and it fits clearly into China’s broader Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and maritime strategy.

First, Piraeus serves as a regional logistics hub for Chinese-linked supply chains. The evidence is explicit on this point. The China-CEE Institute briefing says Piraeus is a gateway for China into the European markets and a focal point in Eurasian economic networks [N6-F4]. The European Guanxi source similarly states that COSCO’s position at Piraeus places it in a position to influence the organisation of inbound and outbound container traffic at the port [N5-F3]. It also says that Piraeus has moved from outside the top 15 European harbours in 2007 to fourth place by 2019, and that the port’s connection to the railway network in 2013 proved particularly significant in accelerating its transformation into a key transit hub and logistics centre for the expanding Asia–Europe trade [N5-F3]. These statements together show that Piraeus is now part of a broader Chinese-linked supply chain network, especially one that links Asia to Europe via the Mediterranean and through Greece’s railway and port infrastructure.

Second, Chinese investment affects Greece’s strategic autonomy and EU connectivity. The evidence suggests a dual logic: modernization and increased connectivity, alongside concerns about dependency and foreign influence. The European Guanxi source notes that Greece had little choice but to pursue further privatisation of the port during the Troika bailout period, and that Chinese actors increasingly emerged as buyers of strategically important national assets [N5-F3]. It also says that the Greek government retained a seat on the board of directors, but COSCO became the majority shareholder [N5-F3]. This partial retention of control suggests that Greece has not fully surrendered strategic autonomy, but it has allowed a major foreign stakeholder to shape the port’s operations. The same source warns that Chinese investments may conflict with European legal frameworks and risk creating dependencies that undermine strategic autonomy [N7-R1]. The U.S. Embassy’s suggestion that Greece could be encouraged to divest parts of its stake is also cited, indicating that Piraeus’s strategic importance has attracted geopolitical attention from outside actors [N5-F3]. In this context, Piraeus is both a source of connectivity and a symbol of dependency, complicating Greece’s balance between European integration and foreign capital.

Third, risks and dependencies remain after increased Chinese involvement. The evidence points to several risks. The European Guanxi source states that expansion into adjacent sectors such as rail transport has stalled due to EU competition rules [N5-F3]. It also reports that local unions and residents have raised concerns about labor rights, environmental damage, and limited local economic spillover [N1-F1]. The evidence shows that the transformation was not just about adding capacity; it was about modernizing infrastructure, improving operational efficiency, broadening connectivity, and embedding Piraeus into broader Eurasian and Chinese-linked supply chains. At the same time, the port’s growing strategic importance has created both opportunities and risks for Greece and Europe.

---

## 1) Operational and infrastructure capacity: major projects, expanded capacity, and modernization

Chinese investment accelerated Piraeus’s infrastructure transformation. The most direct evidence is that COSCO acquired a majority stake in the Piraeus Port Authority in 2016 for €1.5 billion and pledged further €550 million in investments [N1-F1]. The port then moved from an aging facility into a highly coordinated global hub, with terminals extended, deep-water channels dredged, automated equipment gradually put into use, and bridge cranes and yard systems constantly upgraded [N2-F2]. COSCO’s local investment also reached over 10 billion yuan ($1.47 billion), creating thousands of direct jobs and generating tens of thousands of indirect employment opportunities [N2-F2].

A key infrastructure project was the expansion of the Ikonion Container Terminal at Pier I, part of a broader upgrading and expansion of the port [N2-R4]. The port also launched a new park project in April, which will become a modern center integrating sports, leisure, and social activities [N2-R2]. This indicates that Piraeus’s transformation was not confined to container terminals; it included broader port-area redevelopment and smart-city-style modernization.

Handling capacity and terminal efficiency improved dramatically. Piraeus’s container throughput grew from around 680,000 TEUs in 2016 to over 5.6 million TEUs, placing it among the busiest Mediterranean ports [N2-F2]. The port became one of the busiest ports in the Mediterranean, the fourth-largest container port, the second-largest cruise homeport, and the largest ferry port in Europe [N2-F2]. The European Guanxi source attributes this growth to a highly coordinated modern operating system, with once scattered and inefficient operational scenes gradually becoming highly coordinated [N2-F2].

Modernization and digitization evolved over time. The port built a digital monitoring platform covering the entire port area and introduced 5G and artificial intelligence technologies, driving production organization from manual planning to intelligent coordination [N2-F2]. The evidence also points to a “smart green” model, showing that Piraeus is not merely a traditional port but a digitally and environmentally oriented modern port [N2-R3]. This digitization is a key part of the operational transformation.

Workforce and operational efficiency gains are mixed but generally positive. The evidence supports thousands of direct jobs and tens of thousands of indirect employment opportunities [N2-F2]. It also reports that the port’s revenue and profit have continued to grow, reversing a long-term trend of losses [N2-F2].
